What The Ad Blocker Debate Reveals

Cant believe people are skipping over my commercial where I holler into the air about your shit taste in calvin and hobbes while plungers fall onto my face, only one properly sticking to my fat face and suffocating me.

Online content creators will eventually get smart about stuff like this. Linus Media Group for example(First example I could think of) puts ads within their videos and while you could skip them its just a way to force you to see them. I normally skip them and I still know most of their sponsors off the top of my head. Awareness I guess.

I didn't use any ad blockers until Youtube decided it was just way too poor and was throwing an ad at me with every video that I'd watch. I didn't mind when it was every fifth video, or even every third. I've nothing against ads per se. But when everywhere I turn is an ad, yep, you better believe I'm blocking it. Sometimes I'll just pull up Lynx in a terminal window on my work MacBook just to be able to read some news sites without any annoying ads, or pop ups, or click-throughs.

I don't think people would be so turned off by ads if they didn't make them so annoying. When they just pop up or get in the way, making sure I click on them, I'm even more likely to not care about whatever they are trying to sell me. If I see it and it draws intrest, then I get to make the decision to look into it further. If it forces itself under my nose then I most always dismiss it without even knowing what it was trying to get me to pay attention to. Companies are doing it all wrong now. They might get money for the click but they aren't getting my money with a purchase.

If your website is so expensive to maintain that you rely on ad revenue to maintain it, then you're probably doing something really wrong. I see very few sites that should be as complicated and bloated as they are. If your primary revenue is not tied to Internet services, then your site should not be so massive that it requires the ad revenue in order for your business to function.

Voat uses CloudFlare, which is a CDN service based in the United States with infrastructure also in the United States. In its current setup, Voat points its DNS records (voat.co) towards CloudFlare and CloudFlare is able to read, halt or modify communications between people and Voat. CloudFlare is subject to US law (obviously) and, due to the size of CloudFlare and the collapse of the rule of law in the United States, especially in technology, has most likely been subjected to extrajudicial orders demanding data, backdoors, etc. into its infrastructure. CloudFlare, by nature of its ability to modify traffic, holds Voat's SSL keys. CloudFlare not only routes but actively decrypts communications on their way to Voat and is therefore able to be compelled to reveal content of communications bound to Voat.

**It doesn't matter where Voat is incorporated or hosted. Voat has been using CloudFlare since middle June. **Voat tunnels its traffic through an agent that decrypts the traffic in the United States.

So what can we do?

I have an agenda against CloudFlare due to its dishonest promises and terrible behavior/implementation, but I'll ignore that for now and suggest changes in how Voat interfaces within the realm of CloudFlare. CloudFlare offers keyless SSL, which means Voat can still tunnel its traffic through CloudFlare but avoid sharing the content of the communications.

Advantages:

  • No giving up of Voat's SSL key; the SSL key stays with Voat and no one but Voat can decrypt the traffic

  • Voat frees its traffic from being read by foreign adversaries. (its recent incorporation in the United States may jeopardize this point anyway)

Disadvantages:

  • CloudFlare, due to the fact that it no longer holds decryption keys, cannot inject its "check your bits" functionality. Voat will have to take care of it on its own. If I recall correctly, bots keep facing this message so the Voat API is broken right now. Voat should quickly move away from "bot" checking based on JavaScript.

  • Voat needs to setup extra infrastructure ("key server", see link on keyless SSL)
Clearing up some misconceptions: Voat's traffic has been under US eyes for quite some time now
